prompt.en: In the practical radio-horizon model, one antenna is raised from 16 m to 64 m. What happens to that antenna's own horizon contribution?

text.en: It doubles, because square root of height rises from 4 to 8.

feedback.en: The model uses square root of height, not height itself. The other station's contribution is separate.

text.en: It becomes four times larger because height becomes four times larger.

feedback.en: That treats horizon as directly proportional to height and ignores the square root.

text.en: It is unchanged unless transmitter power rises too.

feedback.en: The height term changes even at unchanged power.

text.en: The whole two-station path necessarily becomes twice as long.

feedback.en: Only this antenna's contribution doubles. Add the other station's unchanged contribution before comparing total path estimates.

explanation.en: Separate the changed antenna contribution from the combined path, and remember that terrain can still limit coverage.

prompt.en: A steady VHF path opens along a lake inversion while an HF sky-wave route is poor. Are those observations contradictory?

text.en: Yes; better VHF range is evidence that the same upper-atmosphere change should also help HF.

feedback.en: The described weather-layer VHF path and the ionospheric HF route depend on different parts of the atmosphere.

text.en: No; lower-atmosphere conditions can improve VHF independently of the ionospheric HF route.

feedback.en: A tropospheric enhancement does not establish a useful F-region path at the planned HF frequency.

text.en: Yes; the inversion should provide a comparable path improvement on HF.

feedback.en: A lower-atmosphere enhancement on VHF does not imply a comparable improvement on an ionospheric HF route.

text.en: No; the lake weather change also shifted the ionospheric return point past the HF destination.

feedback.en: The observations do not establish a link between the lake weather structure and the ionospheric return geometry. The paths can change independently.

explanation.en: Interpret the band and physical region together. An opening on one path does not prove that another band is open.

prompt.en: A club credits a taller VHF mast for a longer contact. That trial also used more power during an unusual opening. Which follow-up best tests the height claim?

text.en: Repeat the taller-mast trial at still higher power to separate the mast effect from the opening.

feedback.en: Changing power again adds another influence. It does not separate the height effect from the original power and propagation changes.

text.en: Compare the taller mast during openings with the shorter mast on ordinary days.

feedback.en: That comparison ties height to different propagation conditions. A range difference could come from the opening instead of the mast.

text.en: Compare mast heights on the same route, frequency, and power under comparable ordinary conditions.

feedback.en: Control the other influences and repeat the comparison. This tests height without crediting it for a simultaneous power increase or temporary path enhancement.

text.en: Compare a short local contact on the lower mast with a distant contact on the taller mast.

feedback.en: Changing the route and distance changes the test. Two successful contacts on different paths do not isolate the effect of height.

explanation.en: A longer contact after several simultaneous changes does not isolate the effect of antenna height. Compare like conditions to test that claim.
